analysis.one_liner: Strips states of the power to set production standards for farm goods shipped in from other states, and lets anyone sue to strike down such rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced on June 15, 2023, it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and stayed there through the end of the Congress in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop states and local governments from applying their own production standards to farm products shipped in from other states when those standards go beyond federal law and the laws of the state where the product is made. In practice, that targets state rules on how livestock and other farm animals are raised before slaughter — rules like California's, which voters approved — since a state could still regulate its own farmers but not products crossing its borders from states with weaker rules. It would also create a new federal lawsuit: anyone affected by a state rule on farm goods in interstate commerce, including producers and trade associations, could sue to invalidate the rule and collect damages, and a court would generally have to suspend the rule while the case was pending.
analysis.who_benefits: Large industrial livestock and egg producers gain the most: they could keep using lower-cost confinement and production practices and sell into every state, including states whose voters approved stricter animal welfare or production standards, without changing how they operate. The bill would also give those producers and their trade associations a decade-long window to sue states over existing rules and collect damages, with the rule suspended while the case is pending. Consumers in strict-standard states, and farmers who invested in meeting those standards, would lose the protection and the competitive edge those rules provided.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large industrial livestock and egg producers

how_it_helps.text: It bars state and local governments from imposing production standards on agricultural products from other states that go beyond federal law and the laws of the state where the product is made.

It creates a federal lawsuit route for anyone — including producers, trade associations, and even governments — affected by a state rule on agricultural products in interstate commerce, allowing them to invalidate the rule and collect damages for economic loss.

When such a lawsuit is filed, the court is required to suspend the state rule while the case is pending unless the state can prove by clear and convincing evidence that it is likely to win and that suspending the rule would cause it irreparable harm — a high bar that makes suspension the default.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, state and local governments would pay to defend their rules against a new wave of lawsuits with mandatory injunctions and damages claims, and their taxpayers would bear that cost. Residents of states that voted for stricter production standards would lose those protections for food shipped in from elsewhere, and farmers who had already invested in higher-standard practices would compete against producers who did not.

drawbacks.text: The bill would invalidate rules like voter-approved farm animal welfare standards in states that set them, removing consumers' ability to set production conditions for food sold in their state, and would preempt states even when no comparable federal standard exists.

The mandatory preliminary-injunction provision means any challenged state rule is suspended while litigation proceeds unless the state can prove by clear and convincing evidence it will win — a very high bar — so rules could be effectively nullified for years before a final ruling.

Supporters would argue that a patchwork of differing state production standards raises compliance costs for farmers selling nationally and can shrink the supply of cheaper products; the bill addresses that by imposing a single federal floor rather than leaving states to stack requirements.

The private right of action allows damages for economic loss for 10 years after a regulation takes effect, exposing state and local governments and their taxpayers to prolonged litigation over ordinary regulatory activity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated benefit — relieving farmers from juggling many different state production rules — is real but narrow: it would be achieved by overriding standards that states and their voters chose, backed by a lawsuit system tilted so heavily toward challengers that the rules would be suspended while litigation ran. The cost is that Americans would have no legal channel — state or federal — for production standards on food from other states, and farmers who already invested in meeting those standards would lose that advantage. On balance the bill's effect runs against ordinary people and toward large producers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Agriculture Committee never took the bill up after it was referred there, so it never reached a vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on June 15, 2023 and read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
That referral was the last action the bill ever received — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is listed for the remainder of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

The bill's text would have barred state and local production standards on out-of-state farm goods and created a federal lawsuit route, with a required suspension of state rules while suits are pending, to challenge them.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States with their own farm production standards, including voter-approved animal welfare laws, kept their rules intact, and the producers already meeting those standards kept the advantage of having complied. State taxpayers avoided a standing invitation to litigation and damages claims.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States with their own farm standards kept their rules

for.name: Roger Marshall
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which was read twice and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee.

for.name: 14 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

for.name: Industrial pork and egg producer trade groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported federal legislation to block state farm-animal welfare standards like California's, which raised their costs of selling nationally.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred — no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in its action history.

against.name: Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the bill's last action was the June 2023 referral.

against.name: Animal welfare and humane-farming groups
against.role: Opponents of interstate preemption of animal welfare rules
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against bills like this one, arguing they would overturn state voter-approved farm animal welfare standards.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without any vote, so the fight never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Industrial livestock, egg, and veal producers
industries.note: The bill would let them sell products from lower-standard systems into states with stricter rules like California's, without changing barn design or practices, and give them a lawsuit weapon to strike down and collect damages over such rules. Consumers in those states would lose the standards their voters set, and taxpayers would pay to defend them in court.

industries.industry: Producers that already invested in higher-welfare or higher-standard production
industries.note: These producers would lose the competitive advantage their investments created, since lower-cost producers could sell competing products into the same states without meeting the same standards. Some also sell into multiple states and would gain from facing fewer differing rules.

States and localities would lose the power to set preharvest production standards for food sold within their borders and would face a decade-long window of lawsuits, mandatory injunctions, and damages claims over their agricultural rules.
